d6 and d7 present expert-backed claims that brain-training games do not improve long-term cognition or prevent dementia, while d2 and d5 summarize studies reporting short-term improvements in specific cognitive tasks. These differing outcomes reflect conflicting opinions and research outcomes within the same scope.

The cited evidence collectively shows that while some studies report short-term gains in targeted cognitive skills from playing certain brain-training games, authoritative expert reviews find no strong evidence that such games improve long-term cognition or ward off neurodegenerative decline.

Playing brain-training games can lead to measurable short-term improvements in specific cognitive tasks such as executive function, working memory, and processing speed in randomized trials [d2]. Some analyses also report gains in perception, attention, spatial cognition, and cognitive flexibility after 10–30 hours of video game play [d5]. However, leading experts and expert bodies state there is no strong evidence that brain-training games improve long-term cognition or prevent dementia [d6,d7]. Overall, the evidence supports short-term, task-specific benefits but conflicts with claims of broad, lasting cognitive enhancement from brain-training games [d2,d5,d6,d7].
